  • Deleting a document (or a selection of them) moves it to Trash, a collapsible section at the very bottom of the file explorer — out of the way since it's rarely needed, same as most apps put it. It's not gone. Each item there shows when it was trashed, with buttons to restore it or delete it forever. A toast with "Undo" also appears right after trashing, for a quick reversal without opening Trash at all. Settings → Trash controls how long items sit there before being purged automatically (default 7 days; "Forever" turns off auto-purge so only "Empty Trash" removes anything). Header search (Ctrl/Cmd + K) skips Trash by default — turn on Settings → Trash → "Include Trash in search" to have it surface matches there too (across documents, node text, Notes, tags, and the Pad alike), clearly marked "In Trash"; clicking one reveals it in the Trash section rather than opening it directly, since restoring is a deliberate choice
    • 

  • Searching the file explorer keeps folders visible (showing only matching documents and subfolders, force-expanded) but disables drag-and-drop while a search is active; it only matches document names — for text inside documents, use the header search (Ctrl/Cmd + K) instead
    • 

  • The file explorer's filter box is hidden by default since the header search now covers the same ground; bring it back via the  icon next to "Documents", or Settings → Bars & Menus → File Explorer → Filter box
    • 

  • Drag the thin strip at the file explorer's right edge to resize it
    • 

  • Version history (right-click a document → "Version history", or "More" → "Version history" for the one currently open) keeps automatic checkpoints of a document's past content — not full version control, just lightweight snapshots. A version is captured right before it would otherwise be overwritten, but only once every ~10 minutes of active editing at most, and only if something actually changed, so it won't flood with near-duplicates from every autosave tick. Capped at the last 20 per document, oldest dropped first. "Save a version now" in that panel adds one immediately, useful right before a big rewrite. Restoring an older version is itself non-destructive — whatever was there gets saved as a version first, so restoring is never a one-way trip
    • 

  • If the same document is open as the active one in two tabs or windows of this browser at once (easy to do by accident — duplicating a tab, browser session restore, opening the file twice), a banner appears the moment the other one saves a change, since otherwise whichever tab saves last would silently win with no warning. "Reload latest" discards anything unsaved here and pulls in the other tab's version; dismissing it just clears the banner — your edits here are kept either way, and the other tab gets the same warning in reverse once you save. Documents open here only in the background (not the one on screen) refresh silently instead, since there's nothing unsaved there to protect. This only applies within one browser — a completely different browser, or a different device, never shares storage and can't collide
    • 




          


Sharing & sync


    

  • Signing in (Google or email, from the account button top-right) syncs your documents, folders, and settings to your account, so they follow you to another browser or device. Fully optional — everything keeps working locally without it, and nothing here requires an account except sharing a document with someone else, which needs both people signed in
    • 

  • Profile visibility (Settings → Account, or the Private/Public badge in the account menu itself — either one toggles the same setting) — Private by default. Setting it to Public lets someone find your account by typing your exact email or name when sharing a document with you; Private means your account genuinely can't be found that way, not just hidden behind an extra step. Your name and photo only ever show up in someone's search results once it's set to Public
    • 

  • Share a document — a "Share" chip appears under the title (next to Status/Author/Link) once you're signed in and a document is open; right-click a document in the file explorer → "Share…" does the same, switching to it first if it isn't already open. Type a name or email to search — results only ever include accounts set to Public, shown with their photo/initial, name, and email so you can tell you've got the right person. Click a result to share immediately with whichever access level ("Can view" / "Can edit") is currently selected. The same panel lists everyone who currently has access, with a dropdown to change their role and a × to remove them, at any time
    • 

  • View vs. edit access — a document shared as "Can view" is read-only for that person: their changes won't actually save even if the outline lets them type, since the save itself is rejected without edit access. "Can edit" allows real changes, which sync back to your account the same as your own edits do
    • 

  • Shared — a collapsible section in the file explorer, right after your own documents, listing everything other accounts have shared with you (who shared it, and your access level). Click one to open it as a regular tab. Reopening after closing it or reloading the page means going back to the Shared section and opening it again — a shared document doesn't stay in your tab strip across a reload the way your own documents do
    • 

  • The bell icon next to the account button shows notifications for sharing activity — a new share, an access-level change, or your access being removed. A dot shows how many are unread; clicking a share or access-level notification marks it read and jumps straight to that document
    • 

  • Who's viewing a document — a green "N is here" chip appears next to the Share button while someone else (owner or another collaborator) has the same shared document open, so you're not editing blind. It only shows up on documents that are actually shared with at least one other person
    • 




          


Tabs


    

  • Click a document in the file explorer, or the + at the end of the tab strip → opens it as a tab. Switching tabs keeps each one's undo history, scroll position, and selection independent — it doesn't reset like a plain document switch would
    • 

  • Double-click a tab → rename it
    • 

  •  on a tab, or Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + W → closes the active tab only; the document itself isn't deleted and stays in the file explorer. Closing the last tab leaves the editor empty rather than reopening another document
    • 

  • Drag a tab left or right to reorder the strip
    • 

  • ▾ at the right of the tab strip → search all open tabs by name; ↑ / ↓ + Enter to jump, or click a result
    • 

  • "Reopen tabs on launch" (a Quick Assist toggle — search "reopen tabs") controls whether your open tabs come back next time, or you start with just one
    • 




          


Backing up your data


    

  • Signing in (see "Sharing & sync" above) syncs your documents continuously to your account — a real, live, off-device backup in its own right, not just a way to share. Everything below this still matters even signed in: an account can't help if it's ever deleted or unreachable, so Export in particular is worth keeping as a second, independent copy
    • 

  • Everything is stored locally in the browser, scoped to this exact file. Opening a different copy or a newer version of this file starts with empty storage — that's a browser limitation, not a bug
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Auto-backup to file → keeps a live backup written to a file on disk as you work (Chrome/Edge only — Safari and Firefox don't support this yet). Browsers revoke write permission to that file across a reload or restart as a deliberate security measure, so this can need reconnecting — a chip in the status bar flags it when that happens, and clicking it (or "Reconnect" in Settings) restores it in one click. If you disconnect it yourself from Settings, that same chip stays visible with a plain "Connect backup" prompt rather than disappearing, so there's always a way back to it from the status bar. Since the live file always overwrites itself, a "Backup history" list appears underneath once it's written at least once — up to 5 timestamped snapshots, at least 15 minutes apart so a burst of edits doesn't just fill it with near-duplicates, each independently restorable if a bad edit gets written to the live file before you notice
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Local safety copy → a second copy kept automatically in a separate browser storage area; Restore brings it back if the main storage gets cleared. Not a substitute for Export — it's still inside the same browser
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Undo last restore → appears only after you've used Restore (from a backup file, the Local safety copy, or a Backup history entry above) — a snapshot of whatever was in the app right before that restore, in case the file you picked turns out to have been the wrong one. One level deep: it holds only what was there before your most recent restore, not a full history of every restore you've ever done
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Secure Storage → optional, encrypts AI provider keys and the GitHub Gist token at rest (AES-GCM, passphrase-derived key) instead of storing them as plain text — in this browser and in local backup files. The passphrase itself is never stored anywhere; unlocking derives the key fresh each time, and it only lives in memory for that session — reload the page and you'll need to unlock again to use AI features or Gist auto-sync. There's no recovery if you forget it. Turning it off writes everything back as plain text. Once it's set up, a status-bar chip shows the current Locked/Unlocked state and toggles it in one click — no need to open Settings each session; right-click the chip to jump to the full Secure Storage controls instead. Hide it like any other status-bar item in Settings → Statusbar items if you don't want it there. Unlocking also automatically resumes anything that was paused waiting on it — Auto-rewrite on commit and Gist auto-sync each pick back up on their own the moment you unlock, with no need to redo whatever triggered them originally
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Cloud Backup → optional, pushes the same full backup as "Backup all data" to GitHub Gist or Google Drive instead of a local file, so you can pull it down again from a different browser or computer. GitHub Gist needs a Personal Access Token with the gist scope, pasted into Settings — stored in this browser only, the same as an AI provider key (and covered by Secure Storage above, if that's turned on). Google Drive needs your own free OAuth Client ID from Google Cloud Console; the app only ever sees files it created itself, not the rest of your Drive, and the sign-in token lives in memory only — you reconnect each session, nothing Google-related is written to disk. Both providers find your existing backup automatically by name/description on Save and Load, so there's no ID to copy between browsers by hand. Both are manual push/pull by default — Save fully overwrites the cloud copy with what's here, Load fully overwrites what's here with the cloud copy, no merging either direction. Both also offer "Auto-sync on edit" (off by default) — pushes automatically ~1.2s after edits settle, same timing as Auto-backup to file. Gist's auto-sync persists across reloads (the token is saved) and additionally detects conflicts: if the Gist changed elsewhere since your last Save/Load here, auto-push pauses itself and shows a conflict notice rather than silently overwriting the newer version — resolve it with a manual Save or Load. Drive's auto-sync is session-only, since Drive's sign-in token isn't kept across reloads — it turns itself off with a one-time notice (not a nag) whenever the session connection is gone, and needs reconnecting and re-enabling next time; it has no conflict detection of its own, so treat it as a convenience rather than a safety net if you also edit from Drive on another device. Gist's auto-sync also pauses (with a one-time toast, not a nag on every edit) if the token itself can't be read because Secure Storage is locked — nothing is lost in the meantime since local saves and the safety copy never depend on the vault, and the paused push resumes and sends on its own the moment you unlock, no extra edit needed to retrigger it. Neither AI provider keys nor the Gist token — encrypted or not — are ever included in what gets uploaded to Gist or Drive; only your documents are
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Backup / Restore → the way to move data between files, browsers, or computers, or to take a one-off manual backup. Deliberately only in Settings, not surfaced as a one-click shortcut elsewhere — Restore replaces everything currently in the app, so it's worth the extra couple of clicks to reach it. The header's Export ▾ and Import ▾ buttons are for the current document only (Markdown, Word, OPML, etc.) — Backup/Restore cover all your data
    • 

  • Settings → Data → "Warn if this session isn't backed up" → offers Export or Connect auto-backup if you've made changes this session but neither has run yet. Three modes: Strict shows the browser's own "leave site?" prompt when you try to close the tab, then this dialog if you cancel it — a real last-chance gate, at the cost of that generic browser popup (its wording is fixed by the browser, not by Sakura). Passive skips the browser prompt entirely and shows only this dialog, the next time you switch away from or close the tab — quieter, but a direct close with no prior tab-switch gets no warning at all. Off disables both; the status-bar "⚠ Back up your data" chip (from the reminder setting above) is your only remaining signal. Both this and the status-bar chip stay quiet while you're signed in with sync running normally — an account in that state already is a live, continuous off-device backup, so there's nothing extra to warn about on top of it
    • 

  • Recommended: export before switching to a new version of this file, then import right after opening it
    • 

  • Settings → Data → Reset to default settings → restores appearance/behavior preferences only (theme, toolbar, right-click menu, etc.); your documents and AI settings aren't touched
    • 




          


Notes


    

  • Every node can hold a plain-text note, shown and edited directly underneath the node in the outline itself — there's no separate panel to open. Add or open one via the toolbar ( Note button), right-click → More → Note, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + N
    • 

  • A node with a note shows a small chat-bubble dot — click it to expand the note as its own line directly under the node, editable right there; click again to collapse it (Settings → Editing → "Always expand inline" starts every note expanded instead — the dot still folds it back individually even with that on)
    • 

  • The note line grows automatically as you type multiple lines. Backspace at the start of an empty note deletes it
    • 

  • Right-click the note line for AI Rewrite (rewrites the note's current text) or Delete note
    • 




          


Remarks


    

  • A record of things people said, kept right under the node it concerns: each remark is one line under its node with who said it (a colored initials avatar plus their name), the date, and the remark itself
    • 

  • Right-click any node → Add remark… (on by default in the quick-action row, same place "Add question…" lives) adds one already linked to that node and drops you straight into its text, ready to type
    • 

  • Everything on the line is edited in place: click the name to change who said it (Enter or clicking away saves, Escape reverts), click the date to open the same calendar popover Todo's due date uses (Today/Yesterday presets, plus month navigation for anything else) — useful for logging something after the fact — and type straight into the remark text, which keeps pasted formatting. A node's remarks list newest first
    • 

  • Right-click a remark line for Rewrite with AI (when AI is on) or Delete remark; emptying a remark's text and pressing Backspace removes it too
    • 

  • A small person dot appears on a node with remarks — click it to show or hide them inline (Settings → Layout → "Always expand inline" flips the default)
    • 

  • Deleting a node that has a remark linked to it warns about the orphaned link first, same as it already does for Diagrams
    • 

  • Included in PDF exports (Settings → Export & copy → "Include Remarks in exports", on by default): a remark appears right after the node it's linked to
    • 




          


Q&A


    

  • Questions and answers kept right under the node they're about: right-click any node → Add question… adds a blank question linked to that node and puts the cursor in it. Each one is a bold Q line with its A line underneath, both edited in place and keeping pasted formatting
    • 

  • Right-click a Q&A line for AI Answer (when AI is on — drafts an answer to the question for you to review) or Delete Q&A; emptying the question and pressing Backspace removes it too
    • 

  • A small question-mark dot appears on a node with linked questions — click it to show or hide them inline. The same icon appears next to a folded node's "+N hidden" badge when a question is linked somewhere inside its collapsed subtree, and Where used… lists them alongside the node's other linked content
    • 

  • Settings → Export & copy → "Include Q&A in exports": PDF prints each question right under the node it's linked to, same as a note; questions with no linked node are appended as a final section — bold question, regular-weight answer, unanswered ones marked "No answer provided"
    • 




          


Diagrams


    

  • A real draw.io editor, embedded directly — not a static image. Every diagram belongs to a node in the outline and shows up as a small preview card directly under it; a node can hold any number of diagrams
    • 

  • Right-click a node → Add diagram… to create one already linked to that node — it opens full-screen in draw.io immediately. Click a diagram's preview card (or the small open icon next to its title) to reopen it the same way; the card shows a live thumbnail once it's been saved at least once, and its title can be renamed right on the card
    • 

  • Right-click a node → Generate diagram (listed under "More" by default — Settings → Bars & Menus → Right-click menu adds it to the quick row, or turns it on if your saved menu predates it) turns that node's whole subtree into a rough draw.io diagram automatically, linked to the same node. Meant as a fast first draft to refine by hand afterward in draw.io, not a finished diagram. Caps out at 60 nodes/10 levels deep per generation to stay readable; generate a smaller branch separately if yours is bigger than that.
    • 

  • Generate opens a review screen first — every node in scope, with its proposed shape (plain box, a specific shape like Decision/Datastore/External, or "Edge label"/"Passthrough" to fold it into the diagram rather than draw its own box), whether it's a titled Container, whether its children form a Sequence (chained, vs. fanned out independently), and Sequence direction (vertical/horizontal). Everything's pre-filled with a best guess from the outline's own structure — adjust anything that guessed wrong, select multiple rows for the bulk toolbar at the top, then Generate. Classification is remembered per diagram (not on the node, and never as a document tag — nothing here shows up as a tag chip anywhere else), so regenerating the same scope later reopens pre-filled with whatever you set last time instead of starting over.
    • 

  • Settings → Panels → Diagrams → "Skip review before generating" (off by default) makes generating one click — it renders immediately using that same best-guess (or, on a regenerate, whatever was set last time) with no review screen in between. You can still refine the result afterward directly in draw.io either way.
    • 

  • Only changes saved inside draw.io itself are kept — its own Save button, or Ctrl/Cmd+S, while the editor is open. Closing the full-screen editor (the × button, or Esc) always asks you to confirm you've saved, since there's no way to force a save from outside draw.io's own UI
    • 

  • Multiple pages/tabs within one diagram: draw.io's own page tabs (bottom-left of the editor) work as usual, and every page's content is kept in full when you save and reopen. But the thumbnail, and the figure shown in PDF exports, can only ever show one page — whichever was active in the editor at the moment you last saved. (An earlier version of this tried exporting every page individually behind the scenes; that turned out to actively corrupt the live diagram — deleting a page from it — so it was reverted. Nothing unsafe is attempted here anymore.) A "N pages" badge appears in the full-screen editor's header as a reminder when this applies. If you want more than one page to actually appear in the document, create them as separate diagrams, each under its own node, instead of using pages within one diagram
    • 

  • Give it a title in the field at the top of the full-screen editor; the anchor button next to it moves the diagram under a different node. Choosing "Not linked to a node" there detaches it — an unlinked diagram has no preview card to reopen it from, so only do that if you mean to set it aside
    • 

  • A linked diagram appears as a large figure directly under its node in PDF exports — same treatment as a note image marked "Feature as diagram" elsewhere in Sakura, so there's no visible difference between the two workflows in the output
    • 

  • A small accent-colored square-cluster dot appears next to a node with a linked diagram — click it to show or hide that node's diagram preview cards inline. The same icon appears next to a folded node's "+N hidden" badge when a diagram is linked somewhere inside its collapsed subtree
    • 

  • The full-screen editor's header has Duplicate (same drawing, same status, same node link, titled "(original title) (copy)" — a pure data copy, so it's instant) and Delete (removes the diagram and its node link; the toast's Undo button brings it back for 5 seconds — deleting never touches the node itself)
    • 

  • Each diagram has a status — Draft, In Progress, Review, or Final — shown as a small colored pill in the full-screen editor's header. Click it to cycle to the next status. Purely organizational — nothing else in Sakura reads it (it's not exported or shown in Preview)
    • 

  • Each diagram has a private, one-line note — a reminder to yourself, e.g. "needs sign-off before this is final." Type directly into the small field in the full-screen editor's header — no popup, no separate edit step. Enter or clicking away saves it, Esc discards whatever was typed since it was last saved. Never shown in PDF exports or anywhere outside that editor
    • 

  • Diagrams and Q&A are both included in Sakura's Version History (More menu → Version History for the open document, or right-click a document in the file explorer → Version history) — restoring an older version restores them alongside the outline text. A restored diagram's thumbnail is blank until it's reopened and saved once in draw.io, which regenerates it automatically; the diagram's actual content isn't affected, only the cached preview image. Restoring a version recorded before this existed leaves diagrams/Q&A exactly as they currently are, rather than guessing or wiping them — but if one of those diagrams is anchored to a node that only exists in the newer state you're restoring away from, it becomes unlinked once the outline rolls back (the data itself isn't deleted). The "Version restored" toast names how many diagrams this happened to, if any, so it's never silent
    • 

  • Generate — builds a rough flowchart directly from the outline instead of a blank canvas: the right-clicked node's subtree becomes a real, editable draw.io diagram linked under that node (capped at 60 nodes / 10 levels — a toast asks for a smaller section if you're over that). Layout, sizing, color, and the diagram's XML are always built by deterministic code — AI is only ever asked for a small, whitelisted classification of that same outline (never coordinates, never XML, never a restructured hierarchy), which the deterministic renderer then draws:
  
      
  
    • Structure — boxes tile top-down following the outline's own hierarchy. A node whose children are all childless (a flat list of steps rather than genuine sub-branches) renders as a single vertical chain with sequential arrows instead of fanning out sideways — keeps a long flat step-list narrow rather than blowing out the canvas width, and reads as one continuous sequence rather than alternate paths. That whole chain (the node plus every one of its steps) also gets a background card drawn behind it, tinted to a lighter version of that group's own color rather than one fixed neutral — a pink actor group and a blue UI group each read as their own section, not both sharing the same generic card — so a labeled group of steps ("Webshop Layer" and everything under it, say) reads as one section on the page itself, its own text sitting directly on that card as the section's title rather than getting a redundant box of its own. If those steps are themselves explicitly numbered too ("1 · Simulate order", "2 · Calculate weight", ...), the chain lays out left to right in a row instead of the usual top-to-bottom column — same "these are ordered stages" signal, one level deeper. A node with a real mix of children (some with sub-detail, some without) still fans out normally — unless every one of those children is explicitly numbered ("1. Webshop Layer", "2. ERP Layer", ...), in which case they're read as ordered stages of one flow rather than alternate branches and stack top to bottom instead, each stage's own full subtree rendered normally beneath it, connected from wherever that stage's own content actually ends (not skipping over it) to the next stage's start. Tag that parent node horizontal (or row) to lay those stages out left to right instead — same idea as the numbered-leaf case above, just for stages that still have their own sub-detail, where structure alone can't tell "these are still parallel enough to sit in a row" apart from "these are sequential phases, stack them" (a top-level phase sequence and a same-shaped row of sub-steps look identical on paper). Each stage keeps its own subtree laid out normally beneath it either way — the tag only changes whether stages sit side by side or stacked. All-or-nothing: every sibling in the group has to be numbered for this to kick in, so one numbered aside among ordinary children doesn't pull the whole group into sequence mode by accident. Numbering style is flexible — "1.", "1)", "1:", "1 · ", "1 - " all count, since people number lists differently and the character itself isn't the meaningful part
      • 
  
    • Color — a branch color cycles through 8 hues at every genuine fan-out in the tree, not just the top level, so a real branch point several levels deep (not just the outline's own top-level headings) still gets visually distinct paths with zero AI involved; a chain group's steps stay one uniform color on purpose. An explicit node marker (Confirmed/Issue/Parked/Follow-up/N-A — each its own hue) outranks that, and a node's first tag outranks plain branch color — a tag deterministically hashes to one of 8 reserved hues, so the same tag text always recolors the same way without any keyword list to set up first. All three carry down to untagged, unmarked descendants. Once AI has classified anything in this diagram (see below), a node it left unclassified switches from its branch color to a neutral gray instead — a branch hue has no legend entry to explain it, so once other colors on the page do mean something, an unexplained one would read as a mistake rather than "nothing special here"
      • 
  
    • Box size — width grows with the (possibly-shortened) label up to a cap, and only grows tall enough for two wrapped lines if the label actually needs them, rather than every box defaulting to the same fixed size. A decision diamond gets extra width/height on top of that (a rhombus's angled edges leave much less usable interior than a box's), plus a much tighter label-length budget than every other shape, since even the extra sizing isn't enough room for a full sentence
      • 
  
    • AI's job — one JSON call for the whole scope classifies which nodes are a UI/frontend step, a service call, middleware/integration, a backend process step, an actual persisted data store (kept distinct from an ordinary backend step — only a table/database/record gets the data-store cylinder), an external system, an actor, a genuine decision fork, a pure aside/caveat that isn't a step at all, or a branch that's explicitly out of scope of whatever's being described — each with its own fixed color and, where it helps, its own shape (diamond, cylinder, dashed, dotted). It can also flag a trigger node whose resulting outcomes are written as its siblings rather than its children (something the outline's own hierarchy has no way to connect on its own) and draw that connection as an extra edge, without changing the layout at all. A results-into-two-genuine-paths pattern is usually clearer expressed by nesting the outline itself that way in the first place, though — that's deterministic and doesn't depend on the model noticing anything, where an AI-suggested edge is inherently probabilistic and won't fire on every run. Every one of these is validated against the actual outline structure before it's trusted — a claimed decision only renders as a diamond if the node genuinely has 2+ children in the real tree, regardless of how the model read its own wording, and any classification outside a fixed whitelist is silently dropped. Genuinely fanning/parallel content (rare — most content that touches multiple systems is still a linear sequence, just one that hops between them) can additionally switch the whole diagram to a layered, swimlane-style layout instead. No AI key configured, a locked vault, a provider error, or a response that fails validation all fall back to the plain deterministic version above instead of blocking the diagram or leaving it half-classified — the Generate button spins for the duration of the call so a slower provider still has a visible in-progress state, and the toast afterward says whether AI classification actually applied this run or not
      • 
  
    • Tags — a node tagged decision, database (or db/datastore), excluded, ui, service, middleware, backend, external, actor, or note (a few spelling variants work too — see the source for the full list) sets that node's box type directly, the same shapes AI classification can produce — worth having even when AI didn't run at all, or when AI's own guess should be overridden for a specific node. An explicit tag always wins over whatever AI separately classified that node as. decision only sticks if the node genuinely has 2+ children, same structural guard AI's own decision classification uses, so a stale tag can't produce a diamond with no actual fork under it
      • 
  
    • Edge labels — a node tagged edge-label, placed as a sibling directly between two other nodes at the same outline level, contributes its own text as a label on the arrow connecting those two neighbors instead of becoming a box itself — useful for annotating a transition ("Passes: freight group & qty", "Returns: pricing values") the way a real system-integration diagram would. It never counts toward the 60-node cap and never gets its own layout slot; delete it (or remove the tag) to drop the label again
      • 
  
    • Only categories actually present on the page get a legend entry, drawn to the top-right of the diagram — never a static list of every possible category
      • 
  
    • Generating again for the same node offers to regenerate that diagram in place rather than adding a duplicate — confirms first, since it discards anything changed since inside draw.io; declining leaves the existing one untouched
      • 
  
    • Meant as a rough first draft to refine by hand afterward, not a finished diagram
      • 
  
    

    • 




          


To-Dos


    

  • An app-level task list — not tied to any document or node. One shared list across your whole workspace
    • 

  • Open it from the Hub button in the app bar, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + T; the same shortcut closes it again, and it switches straight to this tab if the panel is already open on a different one
    • 

  • Floating and draggable by its header; drag the thin strip on its left edge to resize its width (remembered between sessions). The  button expands it full-screen the same way Note/Pad/Code do (temporarily overriding your custom width, restored when you leave full-screen)
    • 

  •  Import loads a Sakura To-Dos file — a .json export from another Sakura session or shared by a colleague — adding its tasks to the end of your list with its own Undo toast; any task whose text matches one you already have is flagged (not skipped) in that toast, since text alone can't tell a real duplicate from two tasks that just happen to read the same.  Export in the panel header → PDF prints the full list — Open then Completed — regardless of any active priority/status/due filter, so a filtered view never silently shortens the printout
    • 

  • Type a task and press Enter (or use the + button) to add it — the box grows as you type so long tasks stay readable. Shift+Enter inserts a line break instead of adding the task, both here and while editing an existing task's text
    • 

  • The clock icon next to Export opens Version History for the whole list — same idea as a document's Version History, kept separately since To-Dos isn't tied to any document. A version is saved automatically roughly every 10 minutes a change is made, or click "Save a version now" right before something risky. Restoring one replaces the current list (after saving a checkpoint of what was there first, so restoring is never itself destructive) — keeps the last 20 versions, app-wide
    • 

  • Checking a task off moves it straight to Completed, most-recently-finished first; unchecking sends it back to Open
    • 

  • The Open row shows how many open tasks match the current filter, with a magnifying-glass quick-find icon, sort  and filter  icons at its right edge. Sort covers Manual order, Priority, and Due date; filter narrows the list to one priority level (or tasks with none). Any icon turns accent-colored whenever it's off its default (or quick-find is open) so you can tell at a glance that something's active
    • 

  • Click the magnifying-glass icon to open quick-find and type to search task text, across both Open and Completed. Matches are highlighted and non-matching tasks are hidden entirely (not just dimmed), so the list actually shortens as you narrow it down — this composes with the priority filter, so a priority filter plus a search term shows only tasks matching both. Esc clears the search text first, then a second Esc (or clicking the icon again) closes it; the search always resets when you close the panel. Dragging to reorder still works correctly while filtered — a task dropped next to a visible neighbor lands there in the full list too, even if other hidden tasks sit between them. This searches task text only, live, within the panel — for a version that also opens the panel and jumps to the match from anywhere in the app, Quick Assist's todo: scope still does that
    • 

  • Turn on the select/reorder toggle (checklist icon in the header) to reveal each open task's drag handle, then drag it to reorder. Completed tasks aren't draggable — they're always ordered by completion time
    • 

  • Editing a task's text supports Ctrl/Cmd + Z / Ctrl/Cmd + Y to undo/redo that text edit — its own history, shared across all tasks (app-level, like the list itself) rather than per-task. This covers text edits only: adding, deleting, reordering, and completing tasks keep their existing in-panel Undo toasts instead
    • 

  • Click a task's own background — not its text, and not a checkbox/chip/button, all of which keep doing their own thing on click — to expand it and reveal a spark  AI Rewrite button and a delete button on its chip row, alongside any unset priority/due/link/repeat placeholders. Click the row again to close it — collapsed rows show only the task text (plus any chips that already have a value), so a plain checklist-style task with nothing set takes up as little room as possible. Deleting shows an "Undo" toast, inside the panel itself, for a few seconds in case of a misclick — past that window, Version History (the clock icon) can still bring back a deleted task as part of restoring an earlier snapshot of the whole list
    • 

  • The Completed section header shows a Clear completed button whenever it has tasks (respecting the current priority filter) to remove them all in one action, with its own in-panel Undo toast — a batch counterpart to deleting one at a time. All To-Dos toasts (Undo prompts, export confirmation, AI rewrite errors) show inside the panel while it's open rather than the app's global toast, so acting on one never closes the panel
    • 

  • An overdue count badge can appear on the Hub button itself, in the app bar, whenever you have open, overdue tasks — visible without opening the panel. Toggle it off at Settings → To-Dos → "Overdue count badge" if you'd rather not see it
    • 

  • Priority, due date, and link chips sit below the task text. Priority cycles None → Low → Medium → High on click; due date shows "Today/Tomorrow" or the date, turning red once it's overdue. All three stay visible once set, and only reveal once you click the task to expand it while unset. Clicking the due date chip opens a small calendar popover with Today / Tomorrow / Next week presets up top for the common cases, month navigation for picking any other date, and a "Clear due date" option. Clicking the link chip opens a small popover with two tabs — Web link (an optional display-text field, a URL field, and Save; a bare domain or path is treated as an https:// link automatically) and Link to a node (a search box over your active documents — the same lookup Quick Assist and Global Search use — with results grouped into Documents, for linking the whole document, and Nodes, for one specific spot in it; leave the box empty to browse and pick a document without typing its title first), plus a Remove link option that clears whichever kind is set. A web-link chip shows your display text if you set one, or the link's hostname otherwise; a document-link chip shows the document's title with a plain document icon, and a node-link chip shows that node's own text with a small hierarchy icon, in place of the link-chain icon, so either reads as "jumps within Sakura" rather than "opens a website" — and both stay live, tracking the current title/text rather than a snapshot. Once any kind of link is attached, an open/jump button appears in the row's actions once it's expanded, next to Rewrite and Delete: for a web link it opens a new tab; for a document or node link it switches to that document if needed (scrolling to and briefly flashing the node, the same way backlinks do, when it's a node link specifically). If the node or document has since been deleted, the chip is shown with a dashed outline and clicking either it or the jump button gives a "That node no longer exists" (or "That document no longer exists") toast instead of failing silently
    • 

  • A task can either repeat or hold sub-tasks — never both at once. Click the Repeat chip to cycle None → Daily → Weekdays → Weekly; checking off a recurring task doesn't complete it, it just advances the due date to the next occurrence (a toast confirms the new date), so recurring tasks never pile up in Completed. Once a repeat is set, a small repeat glyph also shows on the due-date chip, even before you've set a due date, so it's clear at a glance that a task recurs
    • 

  • Click a task to expand it, then click Subtask to open an inline field — Enter adds it (Escape cancels), building a small nested checklist under the task with its own checkboxes, an n/300 character counter while typing, and a delete button per item on hover. A progress badge (e.g. "2/4") plus a collapse arrow appear once a task has any sub-tasks; the parent task's own checkbox is disabled and completes automatically the moment every sub-task is checked — you can't check the parent by hand while it has sub-tasks. Setting a repeat on a task removes its sub-tasks' ability to be added (and vice versa, adding a sub-task clears any repeat)
    • 

  • Right-click a task for a context menu — mark complete/open, duplicate the task, copy its text, move it to the top or bottom of the list, expand/collapse its sub-tasks, or delete it. Right-clicking directly on the task's own text, or on a sub-task row, falls through to the normal browser menu instead, so copy/paste and spellcheck still work there
    • 

  • Settings → To-Dos: show or hide the overdue count badge; auto-expire completed tasks after a set number of days; cap how many completed tasks are kept (oldest drop first); choose whether row actions (priority/due/repeat/link chips, Rewrite/Subtask/Delete) stay always visible or only reveal once you click a task to expand it; and whether a task's first sub-task list starts collapsed by default instead of expanded
    • 

  • Typing @ directly in a task's text renders an inline chip: @name for an assignee, @date (ISO date, @today/@tomorrow, or a weekday like @fri) for a date reference, and @status (waiting/blocked/done/review) for status. A suggestion popup appears as you type, offering the date/status keywords plus any names you've already used as @name elsewhere — Arrow keys to navigate, Enter/Tab to accept, Escape to dismiss. These are colored text only — display convenience within the task text, not linked to the priority/due-date/link fields above
    • 

  • #tag renders as a colored tag chip — same autocomplete popup, suggesting tags you've already used. >remark renders everything from the > to the end of the line as a muted italic aside. Both are display only, same as @ tokens
    • 

  • Quick-find already searches the raw task text, so it matches #tags, @mentions, and remark text without any special handling — priority stays a separate structured field with its own dedicated filter
    • 

  • Quick Assist searches your tasks too — type a task's text, or scope it with todo: milk — and clicking a result opens the panel and flashes the match
    • 




          


Feature activation


    

  • Settings →  Features — on/off switches for the handful of capabilities most people actually turn off (To-Dos, AI, Tagging, Quick Assist). Panel-specific extras like Focus, Backlinks, and Hover Toolbar have their own enable switch inside that panel's own Settings section instead — see each one's Help entry below for details. A small dot appears next to "Features" in the rail when any capability here is off, as a reminder
    • 

  • To-Dos — the app-level task list, not tied to any document. Off: the To-Dos tab and its content are hidden from the Hub, and the Settings → To-Dos section is hidden. Existing tasks are preserved
    • 

  • AI Capabilities — the Rewrite, Expand, Summarise, Generate outline, Suggest icon, Suggest tags, and Restructure text features, plus the AI actions inside To-Dos and Q&A. Off: the AI toolbar group, all matching right-click items, and every section under Settings → AI are hidden. Requires a provider API key (Settings → AI → Provider) before anything will run — select a provider and the key hint shows where to get one
    • 

  • Tagging — #tag chips on nodes. Off: the tag toolbar button, right-click action, and tag chips on all nodes are hidden. Tags are still stored in the document data; turning the feature back on restores them
    • 

  • Quick Assist — the search box in the status bar (Ctrl/Cmd+K), which handles both plain-English commands and general search in one place. Off: the shortcut does nothing, the box disappears from the status bar, and any open dropdown closes immediately. Search-result behavior inside it (on/off, category filter, result cap) has its own dedicated section at Settings → Bars & Menus → Quick Assist
    • 

  • Turning a feature off hides every entry point for it (toolbar, right-click, Settings sub-section, Help sub-section). The underlying data is never deleted — toggling a feature is non-destructive in both directions. Feature states are saved alongside your other preferences and restored on the next launch
    • 




          
Start with structure. Refine later.

This permanently deletes your synced documents and settings stored in the cloud for this account, and signs you out everywhere. Sakura

      
Why an outliner — and why Sakura?

      
Think of an outliner as turning your notes into a family tree, instead of a messy pile of paragraphs. Instead of writing left to right, you write in points that tuck inside one another. Here's why that makes life easier:

      

        

          
          

            See the big picture without the clutter
            Five pages of notes usually means scrolling forever to find what you want. In Sakura, you can collapse the details and see just your main headings — like a table of contents. Click one open when you need it.
          

        

        

          
          

            Move things around like LEGO blocks
            In a normal document, moving a section means highlighting, cutting, pasting, and fixing the spacing. Here you just grab one point and drag it — everything tucked underneath comes with it automatically.
          

        

        

          
          

            Bring in the mess, get back structure
            Paste in messy notes or import a Word document — Sakura sorts it into a tree for you, AI-assisted when it needs to be. This part's specific to Sakura, not outliners in general.
          

        

        

          
          

            It keeps you thinking, not just typing
            Plain note-taking lets you write down what someone said without really processing it. An outliner makes you decide, in the moment: is this a new idea, or a detail under the last one? That keeps you actively sorting instead of just transcribing.
          

        

        

          
          

            It grows into a full workspace, not just a tree
            Attach questions and answers, remarks, or a real embedded diagram to any node. Present the whole outline fullscreen with a laser pointer, a running timer, and a whiteboard for sketching mid-talk. Track to-dos alongside it. All still the same outline underneath — nothing here is a separate app bolted on.
          

        

      

      
Not every kind of writing wants this. Flowing essays and loosely connected notes are still better off elsewhere — Sakura's built for things that have a shape: plans, specs, architecture, meeting notes, decisions.

Shape, container, and flow direction for each node — adjust anything that guessed wrong, then generate. This never touches this document's own tags.

Search & Quick Assist

Notes & inline objects

        
    
          
  • Note — per-node, rich text · 
    • 
          
  • Floating, draggable,  to expand full-screen
    • 
          
  • Notes: B I U S, lists, link, table, image paste,  AI rewrite
    • 
          
  • Right-click a node → Add question… / Add remark… / Add diagram… — each lives inline under that node; click the node's dot to show or hide them

To-Dos

        
    
          
  • App-level task list — not tied to any document or node · 
    • 
          
  • Floating, draggable,  to expand full-screen
    • 
          
  • Check off a task to move it to Completed (newest first); turn on the select/reorder toggle to drag-reorder Open tasks
    • 
          
  • Priority and due-date chips below each task; both auto-hide until set or hovered.
    • 
          
  • A task can repeat (Daily/Weekdays/Weekly — completing it just advances the due date) or hold sub-tasks (nested checklist, parent auto-completes when all are checked) — not both at once
    • 
          
  • Right-click a task for a context menu — duplicate, copy text, move to top/bottom, expand/collapse sub-tasks, delete
    • 
          
  • Type @ in task text for inline chips, with autocomplete — @name assignee, @date (e.g. @tomorrow, @fri), @status (waiting/blocked/done/review) — display only
    • 
          
  • # for a #tag (autocompletes from prior tags), > for a muted remark to end of line — both display only
    • 
          
  • Quick-find matches #tags, @mentions, and remark text too — it's a plain substring search over the task text
    • 
          
  • Filter by priority, status, and due date at once (Overdue/Today/Due later/No due date) — all three combine, and the filter menu stays open so you can set several before closing it
    • 
          
  • The same toggle also reveals each task's drag handle. Select multiple open tasks to bulk-set priority, status, or due date, or bulk-complete/delete — each with its own Undo, same as the single-task actions
    • 
          
  • AI (each independently toggleable in Settings → AI → To-Dos AI): header buttons to extract action items from the current document/selection, or generate a status summary of open tasks; a per-task button to break it into 3-6 subtasks — all add directly with Undo, same as Rewrite on each task
    • 
          
  • Settings → To-Dos: auto-expiry, cap on completed tasks, hover vs. always-visible row actions, sub-tasks collapsed by default
    • 
          
  • Searchable from Quick Assist — plain text or todo: milk
    • 
        

      





      

        
AI Features

        
    
          
  •  Rewrite — selected node(s), or highlighted text
    • 
          
  • Right-click → More → Rewrite document for the whole tree
    • 
          
  •  Generate outline · 
    • 
          
  • Restructure text — paste messy/unstructured text → organized into nodes, with wording cleaned up as needed to read well as an outline (won't invent facts not in the source); always opens as a new document; already-structured pastes (bullets/indents) skip the AI call · 
    • 
                    
  •  Suggest icon — picks a fitting emoji prefix
    • 
          
  • Batches over 30 nodes send in sequential chunks
    • 
          
  • Expand node — AI toolbar → expand button (single node selected) → breaks into child nodes
    • 
          
  • Suggest tags — AI toolbar → tag button → applies relevant tags from existing doc tags or new ones
    • 
          
  • Summarise selection — select 2+ nodes → AI toolbar → summarise button → inserts a parent label above them
    • 
          
  • Settings → AI → AI Mode: "Sakura Hosted AI" (sign in, zero setup) or "Bring your own key" (seven built-in providers — Gemini, Groq, Claude, ChatGPT, OpenRouter, Cerebras, GitHub Models — paste your own API key) — all AI features share whichever is active
    •
